Ce passage explique que le châtiment des impies en Enfer est à la mesure de leurs actes, et les commentateurs en donnent la raison dans la phrase « car ils n'espéraient pas de compte ». Selon Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid et la majorité des exégètes, cela signifie qu'ils ne craignaient pas d'être jugés par Dieu et ne croyaient pas à la résurrection. Al-Zajjaj précise que le sens est qu'ils n'espéraient pas la récompense du compte, puisqu'ils ne croyaient pas à la résurrection. Al-Razi donne plusieurs explications, notamment que le mot « espérer » signifie ici « s'attendre à », et que la mention de l'espoir plutôt que de la crainte indique que l'espoir l'emporte dans le compte. Quant à « ils traitaient nos signes de mensonge avec un démenti total », les lecteurs s'accordent à redoubler le son de la lettre dhal dans ce mot, et al-Farra' indique qu'il s'agit d'une forme usitée chez les Yéménites. Le châtiment est dit « conforme » parce que, selon Muqatil, aucun péché n'est plus grave que l'associationnisme et aucun tourment plus grand que le feu. La phrase « Nous avons tout consigné par écrit » signifie que les actes sont enregistrés, soit sur la Tablette gardée, soit dans les registres des anges, selon les avis. Enfin, la parole « Goûtez donc, Nous n'augmenterons pour vous que le châtiment » est unanimement considérée comme la plus terrible des versets sur les gens du Feu, rapportée d'Abd Allah ibn Amr, car leur tourment ne cesse jamais de s'accroître.

Ce passage décrit l'obstination des incrédules : ils ont traité les signes de Dieu par un démenti très violent et poussé à l'extrême. Le verset se rattache à ce qui précède, à savoir qu'ils n'espéraient pas le compte, car ils ont cumulé le refus de la rétribution et le rejet de ce que Dieu a révélé. Les commentateurs s'accordent à entendre par les signes les versets du Coran et ce qu'apportèrent les messagers. Sur le mot « kiddhaban », al-Farra' le tient pour une forme yéménite correcte, un nom d'action de la forme fi''al dérivé de « kadhdhaba », comme khiraq pour « kharraqa », et il en cite un vers à l'appui. Al-Zajjaj et d'autres y voient un nom d'action de la réciprocité, au sens de se traiter mutuellement de menteurs. Ibn 'Atiyya et Abu Hayyan rapportent que la lecture allégée « kadhaban » est attribuée à 'Ali et à 'Awf al-A'rabi, et al-Zamakhshari la rattache à « kadhaba » en s'appuyant sur un vers d'al-A'sha. Al-Zamakhshari et Abu Hayyan proposent plusieurs analyses grammaticales : complément absolu dépendant du verbe sous-entendu, ou du verbe lui-même par sens implicite, ou circonstanciel lorsqu'on lit « kuddhaban » pluriel de « kadhib ». Abu al-Su'ud précise qu'il s'agit d'un démenti excessif, qui explique leur entêtement dans l'incrédulité et dans toutes sortes de fautes. Ibn Kathir et la majorité estiment que le démenti des signes emporte le démenti de toutes les preuves divines sur l'unicité, la prophétie et la résurrection. Le verset se relie ainsi à la suite : le recensement de toute chose par Dieu, puis la parole adressée aux damnés, « goûtez, nous ne vous donnerons que davantage de châtiment », que 'Abdallah ibn 'Amr et Abu Hurayra rapportent comme le verset le plus dur à l'égard des gens du Feu.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset signifie que Dieu a dénombré et consigné toute chose, c'est-à-dire qu'il a exactement compté les actes des hommes, les a déterminés et inscrits sans qu'il ne leur échappe rien, et que cela est rappelé au moment où il est question du châtiment des infidèles dans l'au-delà. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi et Ibn 'Atiyya comprennent le mot livre comme une inscription précise dans la Table gardée, tandis qu'al-Razi voit dans ce terme une insistance sur la certitude du savoir divin, adaptée à la compréhension de ceux qui s'en tiennent à l'apparence, car ce qui est écrit peut disparaître alors que la science de Dieu ne disparaît jamais. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan et al-Nasafi en font un complément de manière, c'est-à-dire un écrit fixé dans la Table ou dans les registres des anges gardiens. Al-Shinqiti rattache la chose aux actes des serviteurs et y voit la preuve de l'étendue de la science divine jusqu'aux détails, tandis qu'Ibn 'Uthaymin y voit aussi bien les actes de Dieu que ceux des hommes. Ibn 'Ashur explique que l'expression signifie une grande rigueur de comptabilité. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le fait que cette phrase est une incise qui relie la rétribution à la connaissance totale, et que le verset suivant, ô vous qui goûtez, nous n'augmenterons pour vous que le tourment, est considéré par Ibn 'Abbas, Abd Allah ibn 'Amr et Abu Barza comme le plus sévère à l'égard des gens du feu. Tous admettent que la sanction est conforme aux actes des incroyants, qui ne espéraient pas le compte et traitaient les signes de Dieu de mensonges.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset s'adresse aux damnés au moment du châtiment : il leur est dit de goûter la rétribution de leurs actes, et Dieu n'ajoutera à leur tourment que de la souffrance, ce qui est une réprimande et une menace en accord avec leur incroyance et leur déni. Al-Tabari, citant Qatada, et Ibn Kathir, citant Abdallah ibn Amr, rapportent que ce surcroît de châtiment est sans fin, les damnés étant « en surcroît de tourment à jamais ». Al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir et d'autres voient dans le mot « goûtez » l'expérience directe du supplice, et disent que la punition est proportionnée à leurs œuvres. Ils ajoutent que leur tort tenait à ce qu'ils « n'espéraient pas le compte », c'est-à-dire qu'ils ne croyaient pas à la résurrection ou ne craignaient pas le jugement, comme le rapportent al-Tabari, Mujahid et Qatada. Quant au déni des signes divins, al-Tabari et d'autres l'entendent comme le rejet des preuves et des arguments de Dieu. Sur le mot « kidhdhaban », la majorité le lit avec la gémination comme nom d'action de « kadhdhaba », tandis qu'al-Kisa'i et d'autres l'admettent aussi sous forme allégée, et al-Zamakhshari y voit un nom d'action de « kadhaba ». Ibn Atiyya et al-Qurtubi notent que ce verset est tenu pour le plus sévère du Coran à l'égard des damnés, en se fondant sur le hadith d'Abu Barza, bien que la chaîne en soit faible selon Ibn Kathir. Les savants s'accordent donc sur le fond, et diffèrent surtout sur les détails linguistiques et de lecture.

Les commentateurs expliquent que le verset « Les pieux auront certes une réussite » signifie que ceux qui craignent Dieu en obéissant à Ses ordres et en évitant Ses interdits obtiendront le salut et l'entrée au Paradis, et qu'ils atteindront ce qu'ils recherchaient. Ibn Abbas rend « mafaz » par « lieu de promenade », tandis que Qatada et Mujahid y voient la délivrance du feu et la miséricorde après le châtiment. Le verset précise cette réussite par les jardins et les vignes : al-Tabari explique que les « hada'iq » sont des vergers clos de murs où poussent divers arbres, et que la mention des vignes vient en sus. Les « kawa'ib » sont les jeunes femmes à la poitrine ferme et saillante ; Mujahid et al-Dahhak les identifient aux vierges, et les « atrab » sont de même âge selon Ibn Abbas, Qatada et Ibn Zayd. Sur la coupe « dihaq », les avis divergent : pleine et débordante pour Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan et Qatada ; successive pour Sa'id ibn Jubayr et Mujahid ; pure pour Ikrima. Il est admis que les habitants du Paradis n'y entendent ni futilité ni mensonge, et al-Kisa'i lisait « kadhdhaban » avec une forme allégée, ce que d'autres rattachent au sens de « tadhib ». Quant à « 'ata'an hisaban », la majorité y voit un don suffisant, tandis que Mujahid le rapporte à une rétribution proportionnée aux œuvres.

Les commentateurs expliquent que le « mafaz » de la parole divine « Pour les pieux, il y a certes un mafaz » désigne la réussite, l'atteinte du but et le salut hors du Feu, comme le disent Mujahid, Qatada, al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir. Ibn Abbas et al-Dahhak l'entendent comme un lieu de promenade. Le verset « jardins et vignes » est présenté comme une explication de cette réussite ou comme une apposition : les jardins sont des vergers entourés de murs, et la vigne est citée à part pour sa valeur et son abondance, al-Tabari précisant que les pieds de vigne sont sous-entendus.

Les « kawaʿib » sont, selon la plupart, des jeunes femmes à la poitrine ferme et bien dressée, al-Dahhak y voyant des vierges. Les « atrab » sont de même âge, ce que confirment al-Qurtubi et Ibn Atiyya. Pour la coupe « dihaq », les avis convergent largement sur le sens de pleine, avec Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan et Qatada ; Said ibn Jubayr et Mujahid y voient une coupe qui se succède, et ʿIkrima une boisson pure.

Quant à « ni vain propos ni mensonge », les opinions diffèrent : Ibn Abbas parle de paroles vaines, al-Suddi de serments au moment de boire, Mujahid d'insultes, al-Hasan de désobéissance. Pour le mensonge, Said ibn Jubayr comprend qu'ils ne se mentent pas entre eux, al-Hasan y voit une querelle et Qatada une faute. Al-Kisa'i lit « kidhaban » sans redoublement, tandis qu'al-Tabari préfère la forme avec redoublement. Ibn Kathir conclut que le paradis est exempt de toute imperfection.

Enfin, le don divin « ʿata'an hisaban » est compris par al-Zamakhshari et Ibn Kathir comme un don suffisant et abondant, et par Mujahid comme proportionné aux œuvres. Les lectures de « Rabb » et « al-Rahman » varient, et les commentateurs en exposent les raisons sans trancher.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset fait partie de la description des jardins réservés aux pieux. Les « kawāʿib » sont des jeunes femmes à la poitrine ferme et saillante, comme un osselet, et les « atrāb » sont celles qui ont le même âge. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Zayd et Ibn Kathir expliquent que les kawāʿib sont des jeunes femmes à la poitrine ferme et que les atrāb sont des compagnes du même âge. Al-Dahhak y voit des vierges, opinion rapportée par Qays ibn ʿAsim, tandis qu'Ibn Jurayj et Qatada insistent sur la fermeté de la poitrine. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi et al-Baghawi rattachent ce verset aux descriptions du paradis, et al-Razi comprend les atrāb comme des compagnes du même âge. Ibn ʿAshur note que cette égalité d'âge peut concerner les femmes entre elles ou leur relation avec leurs époux. Tous s'accordent sur le fait que ces compagnes relèvent des délices du paradis et de sa perfection. Ibn Kathir cite un hadith d'Abu Umama sur les kawāʿib atrāb, et al-Alusi rapporte que les femmes du paradis sont âgées de seize ans selon certains commentaires. Al-Tabari ne tranche pas entre ces opinions.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset décrit le bonheur promis aux pieux, et que la coupe « dihaq » est une coupe pleine, débordante. Cette lecture, la plus répandue, est transmise par Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan et Ibn Zayd, qui disent que le breuvage remplit le vase sans en rien laisser vide. Al-Tabari rapporte qu'Ibn 'Abbas demandait à son serviteur de lui servir une coupe « dihaq » et qu'il déclarait celle qui arrivait pleine être précisément ce sens. Sa Racine évoque la pression et le serrage, ce qu'explique al-Qurtubi, qui ajoute que le sens de « succession » rejoint celui du contenu serré. Sa'id ibn Jubayr et Mujahid, cités par Ibn Kathir et al-Mawardi, la comprennent comme une suite de coupes qui se succèdent, tandis qu'Ikrima la tient pour un breuvage pur. Al-Razi retient en premier lieu le sens de plénitude, qu'il appuie sur l'usage des Arabes, et évoque aussi la pureté. Le Zamakhshari y voit la boisson elle-même, et Ibn 'Ashur note qu'elle est appelée « coupe » par une figure usuelle. Le verset enchaîne sur l'absence de paroles vaines et de mensonge dans le Paradis : les commentateurs disent que les boissons de l'au-delà n'enivrent pas comme celles d'ici-bas. Les lectures de « kadhdhaban », au redoublement ou non, sont discutées par al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Qurtubi, sans que l'un d'eux tranche absolument.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset décrit la récompense des pieux après l'évocation du sort des rebelles : dans le Paradis, ils n'entendent ni propos vains ni mensonge. La plupart s'accordent à dire que leurs oreilles sont préservées de toute parole creuse ou fausse, de sorte qu'ils ne se querellent ni ne se contredisent. Ibn 'Abbas et Qatada, suivis de Sa'id ibn Jubayr, entendent le lagha comme la parole futile ou le mensonge, tandis que Mujahid y voit l'injure, al-Hasan la désobéissance et al-Sudi le serment prononcé en buvant du vin. Quant au kidhdhaban, Sa'id ibn Jubayr l'interprète comme le fait de se traiter mutuellement de menteur, al-Hasan comme la dispute et Qatada comme la faute. La plupart lisent la forme redoublée, alors qu'al-Kisa'i lit la forme simple, au sens de mensonge ou de mutuelle dénégation. Al-Tabari préfère la lecture redoublée sans exclure l'autre. Ibn Kathir considère que les paroles qui n'ont pas d'utilité ni de faute sont absentes du Paradis, qui est la demeure de la paix. Al-Razi estime que le pronom « là » renvoie à la coupe ou au Paradis, et que le verset nie entièrement l'écoute du mensonge. Ibn 'Ashur y voit une manière de préserver la boisson céleste de l'agitation qui accompagne le vin d'ici-bas.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset conclut la description de la récompense des pieux : Dieu les rétribue par une récompense et leur accorde un don, par pure grâce. Le mot « hisab » est compris par la plupart comme « suffisant et abondant », car on dit « aḥsabanī al-shay’ » pour signifier qu’une chose suffit, tandis que d’autres y voient une mesure proportionnée à leurs œuvres. Al-Tabari, Mujahid et Qatada rapportent que le don est abondant et que la bonne action est multipliée par dix ou par sept cents, la hausse au-delà du juste salaire étant elle-même une grâce divine. Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari et al-Baydawi retiennent le sens de suffisance et d’abondance, tandis qu’al-Razi énumère plusieurs sens, dont celui d’une récompense due par promesse et d’une grâce qui n’est pas due. Sur le plan de la lecture, certains lecteurs ont employé le génitif pour « rabb » et le nominatif pour « al-Rahman », et al-Tabari préfère le génitif à cause de sa proximité avec « rabbika ». Ash-Shawkani et Ibn Kathir soulignent que ce don est une félicité durable qui ne cesse pas. Les commentateurs s’accordent sur le fait que le don est une grâce de Dieu accordée selon les œuvres, tout en divergeant sur le sens précis de « hisab », sans que l’un des sens ne soit tranché comme seul valable.

Ce verset affirme que Dieu est le Seigneur des cieux et de la terre et de ce qui se trouve entre eux, le Miséricordieux dont la miséricorde embrasse toute chose, et que, le jour de la Résurrection, les créatures ne peuvent Lui adresser la parole sans Sa permission. Les exégètes divergent sur l'antécédent du pronom de « ne possèdent pas » : Ibn 'Abbas, selon la transmission de 'Ata', et al-Kalbi estiment qu'il renvoie aux polythéistes, qui ne s'adresseront pas à Dieu, tandis que les croyants intercéderont et seront exaucés ; al-Qadi y voit les croyants, qui n'ont pas le droit de contester le jugement équitable de Dieu ; al-Razi, al-Nasafi et Ibn 'Atiyya l'étendent à l'ensemble des habitants des cieux et de la terre, aucun d'eux ne pouvant interpeller Dieu au sujet de la récompense ou du châtiment. Quant aux lectures, elles varient entre le nominatif et le génitif pour « Rabb » et « al-Rahman » ; Abu 'Ubayd, suivi par Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Zamakhshari, préfère le génitif pour le premier mot, proche de « ton Seigneur », et le nominatif pour le second, plus éloigné ; al-Tabari juge toutes ces lectures correctes. Tous s'accordent à situer ce discours au jour du Jugement, où la parole est soumise à l'autorisation divine. Le « Rouh » qui se tient debout avec les anges en rangs suscite en revanche de nombreuses opinions : Ibn Mas'ud et, selon une transmission, Ibn 'Abbas y voient un grand ange ; al-Sha'bi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr et al-Dahhak, Gabriel ; Mujahid et Abu Salih, une créature à figure humaine qui n'est ni ange ni homme ; al-Hasan et Qatada, les descendants d'Adam ; Zayd ibn Aslam, le Coran ; al-Tabari refuse de trancher. La plupart rapportent « dire juste » à la profession de foi « il n'y a de dieu que Dieu », tandis que Mujahid et al-Dahhak y voient la vérité.

Ce verset décrit le jour du Jugement, où l'Esprit et les anges se tiendront en rangs, et où nul ne parlera sauf celui que le Miséricordieux autorise, et qui dira une parole juste. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens général : c'est un moment de crainte révérencielle où la parole est soumise à une double condition, l'autorisation divine et la justesse de ce qui est dit. Quant à l'identité de « l'Esprit », les avis divergent. Ibn Mas'ud et Ibn 'Abbas, rapporté par Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi, y voient un ange d'une grandeur extraordinaire, tandis que al-Sha'bi et al-Dahhak y voient Gabriel, avis que retient al-Razi et que soutient al-Qadi. Mujahid et Abu Salih le décrivent comme une créature à l'image des humains, ni anges ni hommes. Al-Hasan et Qatada disent qu'il s'agit des fils d'Adam, tandis qu'Ibn Zayd y voit le Coran. Al-Tabari refuse de trancher entre ces opinions, et Ibn Kathir penche pour les fils d'Adam. Sur la parole juste, Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrima et Abu Salih l'entendent comme la profession de foi « Il n'y a de dieu que Dieu », al-Dahhak et Mujahid comme la vérité, et al-Hasan comme la déclaration que nul n'entre au Paradis sans miséricorde ni en Enfer sans ses œuvres. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Razi retiennent que la parole doit être à la fois permise et juste. Le verset se conclut sur le jour véritable, où celui qui le souhaite se fera par ses œuvres un chemin de retour vers son Seigneur.

Les commentateurs expliquent que « ce jour-là, le jour de la vérité » désigne le Jour de la Résurrection, un événement certain sans aucun doute. Quant à « quiconque le veut, qu'il se fraie vers son Seigneur un retour (ma'ab) », cela signifie que celui qui veut être sauvé doit se choisir un retour digne auprès de son Seigneur par la foi, l'obéissance et les bonnes œuvres. Qatada interprète le mot ma'ab comme un chemin, tandis qu'al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir retiennent le sens de lieu de retour. Pour « Nous vous avons avertis d'un châtiment proche », la majorité y voit le châtiment de l'au-delà, car tout ce qui doit venir est proche. Qatada et Muqatil y voient toutefois le châtiment ici-bas, comme la défaite de Quraysh à Badr. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que « le jour où l'homme verra ce que ses mains ont avancé » signifie que chacun verra ses actes, bons ou mauvais. Al-Hasan et Qatada entendent par « l'homme » le croyant, tandis qu'Ata' et d'autres en font un sens général. Le mécréant souhaitera alors être poussière. Ibn Kathir et al-Tabari rapportent à ce propos des récits d'Abu Hurayra et d'Ibn Amr sur le jugement des bêtes, qui sont ensuite changées en poussière, ce qui fait désirer au mécréant d'être semblable à elles. Al-Razi et al-Qurtubi signalent aussi que certains voient en ce mécréant Iblis, qui méprisait l'argile dont Adam fut créé. Al-Razi note enfin que ce passage ne nie pas que les actes soient cause de récompense ou de châtiment. Tous s'accordent sur l'exhortation à faire le bien avant qu'il ne soit trop tard.

Ce verset avertit d'un châtiment proche, celui de l'au-delà, car tout ce qui doit venir est proche. Ce jour-là, chacun voit ce que ses mains ont accompli, de bien ou de mal, et l'incroyant souhaite être poussière. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur l'avertissement et sur la grande détresse qu'il exprime. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi rapportent que le mot « l'homme » désigne l'ensemble des humains, ou le croyant selon al-Hasan et Qatada, qui explique que le croyant voit ses œuvres sans savoir son sort final. Pour al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir, l'incroyant voit son œuvre et désire ne jamais avoir été créé ni ressuscité. Le souhait « être poussière » s'explique, selon plusieurs récits transmis d'Abu Hurayra et d'Ibn Umar, par le fait que les animaux sont jugés entre eux puis transformés en poussière, ce que l'incroyant envie. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi et Ibn al-Jawzi rapportent aussi cette explication. Certains, comme al-Baghawi, al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy et Abu Hayyan, rapportent que l'incroyant pourrait être Iblis, qui méprisait Adam créé d'argile, et qui souhaiterait alors être fait de la même matière. Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi jugent plus juste de considérer que le terme vise tout incroyant. Les commentateurs divergent donc sur l'identité de « l'homme » et de « l'incroyant », et sur le sens exact de la poussière, mais s'accordent sur la gravité de l'avertissement.
en: The surah opens by describing how the disbelievers question and dispute among themselves about the great news. The commentators differ on what this great news is. Mujahid and Ibn Abbas, as reported by al-Tabari, identify it as the Quran, while Qatada and Ibn Zayd identify it as the resurrection after death and the Day of Judgment. Ibn Kathir prefers the resurrection, since the verse goes on to say that people are divided about it, and death itself is not disputed. Most scholars, including al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya, explain that the interrogative form expresses magnification of the matter rather than a request for knowledge. Al-Sam'ani notes that the Prophet's call to monotheism and the resurrection led people to ask one another what he had brought. Al-Razi observes that the disputed matter may be the resurrection in general, in which the disbelievers were divided between deniers, doubters and those who accepted a spiritual afterlife. The repeated words 'no, they will come to know' are read by most as a warning that they will learn the truth at death or on the Day of Resurrection. The verses that follow list the earth, the mountains, sleep, night, day, the heavens, the rain and the plants as signs of God's power to raise the dead.

The verse asks what the disbelievers are asking one another about, namely "the great news," and the commentators differ on what it is. Mujahid, Ibn Abbas and Muqatil say it is the Quran; Qatada and Ibn Zayd say it is the Resurrection and the Day of Judgment; al-Hasan says it is prophethood. Al-Farra' and Ibn Kathir prefer the Resurrection, since people are divided over it between believers and deniers. All agree that the interrogative form is meant to magnify the matter rather than to seek information, and that "about which they differ" means people are split between those who reject and those who doubt.

Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the pronoun "they ask" may refer to the disbelievers alone, or to believers and disbelievers together: the believer asks to grow in certainty, the disbeliever to mock. On "Nay, they will come to know," al-Dahhak reads it as the disbelievers learning the outcome of their denial and then the believers learning the outcome of their faith; al-Hasan and most others take it as one threat following another. The following verses, the commentators explain, show God's power to resurrect through the earth made a cradle, the mountains as pegs, the night as a garment, the day for livelihood, the heavens, and the rain that brings forth grain, plants and gardens.

Readers differ between the forms "ya'lamun" and "ta'lamun"; this difference does not change the main meaning.

God reports that the polytheists were asking one another about "the great news", the momentous message brought by the Prophet ﷺ, on which they were divided between believers and deniers. The commentators agree that this questioning expresses amazement and exalts the subject rather than seeking real information. The divine reply, "No! They will soon know", repeated twice, is a stern warning and a reinforced threat. Opinions differ on what the great news is. Mujahid and most scholars identify it with the Quran, Qatada and Ibn Zayd with the Resurrection and the Last Day, while al-Zajjaj mentions the Prophet's command. As for the disagreement, Qatada explains that it is between believers and deniers, Yahya ibn Salam between Muslims and polytheists, and al-Tabari notes that people split into two camps, though none disputed the reality of death. Regarding the repeated "kalla", most read it as simple emphasis, whereas Ad-Dahhak assigns the first to the disbelievers and the second to the believers. The commentators then link the following verses on the earth as a cradle, the mountains as pegs, the night as a garment and the day as a time of livelihood to the proof of God's power over resurrection. They also differ on the "mu'sirat": Ibn Abbas and Mujahid take them as winds, al-Farra' and Ibn Kathir as clouds about to rain, and others as the heavens. Overall, the verse affirms that people disagree about a clear truth, and that certain knowledge of it will certainly come.

This verse opens the passage in which the disbelievers ask about "the great news", and the reply "No! They will soon know" serves as a rebuke and a warning that they will learn the outcome of their denial. The commentators agree that "kalla" is a rejection and reproach, and that "they will know" is a threat implying that what they mock is certainly true. The repetition is explained by al-Hasan as one threat following another, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and others note that "thumma" signals the second warning is stronger than the first. On "the great news", Mujahid, Qatada and Ibn Kathir take it to mean the resurrection after death, Ibn Kathir preferring this view; Mujahid in another report, Muqatil and al-Farra' say it is the Qur'an, and Ibn Zayd says it is the Day of Judgment. On their disagreement, Qatada explains it as belief versus disbelief, while Yahya ibn Salam says it is between Muslims and polytheists. Opinions also differ on who the second warning addresses: al-Dahhak assigns the first to disbelievers and the second to believers, whereas the majority, including Ibn Kathir, apply both warnings to the disbelievers.

The commentators explain that this verse answers the Quraysh, who were questioning and disputing about the great news, and it rejects their stance: the matter is not as they claim, and they will come to know the consequences of their denial. The repetition of the rejection and the threat serves to emphasise it. Al-Hasan sees it as one warning following another, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the particle thumma signals that the second threat is stronger than the first. As for what the great news is, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil take it to be the Quran, while Qatada, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to be resurrection after death. Most say the disagreement is between believers and disbelievers. Regarding who will know, al-Dahhak assigns the first warning to the disbelievers and the second to the believers, but most exegetes hold that the threat is entirely for the disbelievers. Al-Tabari understands that they will know, when they meet God, that their claim was false, and Ibn Uthaymin describes a certainty of knowledge gained by witnessing the events. The majority reading uses the third person, while Ibn Amir and al-Hasan read the second person, and Ibn Ashur notes the higher rank of the second threat.

The commentators explain that God reminds those who deny resurrection of His manifest favours so that they may recognise His power. He says: Have We not made the earth a bed (mihad), a spread and a stable resting place on which people move and act? Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand mihad as a carpet or level floor, and say that the mountains were set in the earth like tent pegs so that it would not shake with its inhabitants. The commentators agree that these favours show God's power and wisdom: the One who created such great things can certainly bring the dead back to life. As for 'We created you in pairs', al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take it to mean male and female, while others take it to mean differences of colour, form and language, and al-Qurtubi extends it to every pair of opposites. Sleep is subat, a rest and a cessation of activity; the night is a garment that covers people with its darkness; the day is a time for livelihood, when people work and move about. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi note that mihad can be a noun for what is prepared, like the cradle (mahd), a reading attested by Mujahid and Isa. Ibn Juzayy and al-Qasimi stress that these verses prove both God's oneness and the possibility of resurrection, since the One who does all this is not unable to raise the dead. The commentators agree that these verses are an argument addressed to the Quraysh who denied the return after death.

The commentators explain that this verse recalls the blessing of the mountains, which are likened to tent-pegs driven into the earth so that it does not sway with those upon it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya agree on this general sense, and read it as evidence of the divine power that makes resurrection possible. Al-Sam'ani reports from Ibn 'Abbas the account that the earth began to shake before the mountains were created, and they then steadied it. Al-Razi holds that the mountains prevent the earth from moving, and links this to the image of the peg that holds a tent. Al-Zamakhshari presents it as an argument for the power of the Creator. Al-Alusi explains that the image means the earth is anchored by mountains as a house is anchored by its pegs, and notes that some preferred a reading in which the mountains secure human life, which he judges contrary to the apparent meaning. Ibn 'Ashur sees the comparison as possibly concerning only the form or the function, with the mountains helping to stabilise the earth's motion within the atmosphere. The commentators do not differ on the main sense, but on the details of the comparison and on the idea of the earth's sway.

The commentators explain that, within the list of God's blessings addressed to the polytheists, the verse "We created you in pairs" means in its plainest sense that God created human beings male and female, so that each may find rest in the other and offspring may continue. Al-Tabari, citing Qatada, adopts this reading and adds that the pairs include tall and short, handsome and plain. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi hold that the word covers every pair of opposites, such as beautiful and ugly, long and short, since such variety allows for trial, so that the grateful believer may give thanks and the less favoured may be patient, and so that each thing is known through its opposite. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari understand the pairs as differing kinds in colour, form and language. Al-Sam'ani reads the word in the sense of mutual harmony and affection, treating the man and the woman, like heaven and earth or night and day, as complementary pairs. Ibn Kathir links the verse to the love and mercy between spouses. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verb "create" refers here to the constitution of persons themselves, and that the paired form recalls the Creator's power to bring back what He has made. These commentaries draw no legal ruling from the verse, which belongs to the argument for resurrection and divine unity.

The commentators explain that God made sleep a sabat, meaning a cessation of movement and activity and a rest for the body, listed among the blessings that display His power. Most, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, take the sense of rest and stillness, noting that the root means cutting off, which is why the Sabbath day was named for the cessation of work. Al-Zajjaj and al-Nasafi stress the stopping of activity, while al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Abu al-Su'ud report that sleep resembles death and link the verse to the verses about God taking souls at night. Al-Razi holds that this death should be understood as the suspension of the outer senses rather than the departure of the soul. Ibn al-Qayyim adds two benefits of sleep: heat moves to the belly to aid digestion, and the limbs wearied by work are rested. Al-Mubarrad understands sabat as a light sleep that one can shake off, and some take it as a deep torpor, but al-Razi finds this reading weak given the context of blessings. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the root means cutting and that rest follows from it, and he disputes that the verb itself means rest. Al-Alusi likewise prefers the meaning of death as best suited to the context.

The commentators explain that God, in this part of the chapter, enumerates His favours to the disbelievers, and among them is the verse 'And We made the night a garment'. The plain meaning is that the darkness of the night covers people and conceals them as a garment covers the one who wears it, so that they rest from the activity of the day. Most commentators hold this apparent meaning. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir say that the night covers people with its darkness, and Ibn Kathir cites a verse of Dhu al-Rumma comparing the night to a garment. Ibn Kathir, al-Jalalayn and al-Nasafi add that it hides people from sight. Al-Razi and al-Alusi add that it shelters someone fleeing from an enemy or planning a night raid, or hides what one does not want others to see. Qatada, al-Suddi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr explain it as tranquillity and rest, a view that Ibn al-Jawzi also reports. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi emphasise protection, and al-Razi adds that the night enhances a person's beauty and eases bodily weariness. The commentators do not settle between these readings, which largely converge: the night is a covering, a rest and a shelter. Ibn 'Ashur notes that some see in the verse a refutation of dualists who make the night a god of darkness, and he cites al-Mutanabbi on the point. Overall the commentators agree on the general sense without judging among the explanations of the word 'libas'.

The commentators explain that « And We made the day a time for livelihood » is part of a series of divine favours that the passage lists in order to press the argument against those who deny resurrection and the oneness of God. For most of them, the word ma'ash means the time in which one lives, moves about, works and seeks one's means, so the day is the time of activity and the search for sustenance, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report. Some set the day, the night and sleep side by side: sleep is rest and a cessation of labour, the night is a covering that veils people, and the day is the time of life, waking and work, as Ibn 'Ashur observes, seeing in this pairing a stylistic antithesis.

On the grammatical nature of the word, opinions differ. Many take it as a verbal noun meaning life or the act of living, with an implied sense of a time for subsistence. Others, such as al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi, take it as a noun of time or place, meaning the day is when one lives. Al-Zamakhshari draws from this that the day stands opposite sleep, which he treats as a kind of death, while al-Alusi considers both readings acceptable.

The commentators agree that the day is the condition that allows people to disperse and earn their living, but they differ in how they describe this: some speak of gain and food, others of seeking God's bounty. None of them preferred one formulation over another, and they are not mutually exclusive. The verse remains, above all, a reminder of the day's benefit.

In this verse God mentions another of His favours to mankind: He built above you seven strong heavens. The commentators largely agree that the seven strong ones are the seven heavens, described as strong for the solidity of their creation, so that the passing of time does not wear them down and they have no cracks or rifts. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir adopt this reading, while al-Baghawi cites a report attributed to Muqatil that the thickness of each heaven is a five-hundred-year journey. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi repeat this view, and Ibn Juzayy presents the verse as proof that the One who created such vast things can also raise the dead. Al-Zamakhshari explains the verb 'built' as a way of conveying height and firmness, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that Arabs called the roof of a house a building. Most exegetes identify the 'brilliant lamp' with the sun: Ibn 'Abbas takes it as light, Mujahid as shining, and al-Hasan as heat. On the 'pressing clouds' (al-mu'sirat), the majority read them as clouds that are ready to release rain, like a young girl approaching puberty. Mujahid, Qatada and, in one transmission, Ibn 'Abbas take them to be winds, while al-Hasan and Qatada take them to be the heavens. Al-Tabari prefers the sense of clouds, and Ibn Kathir considers it the most apparent. The 'pouring water' (thajjaj) is, for most, water poured out steadily, and Ibn Zayd understands it as abundant water.

The commentators explain that God, after the disbelievers denied the resurrection, lists some of His favours, and here says that He made the sun a blazing, shining lamp. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi agree that the lamp is the sun, and that the word wahhaj means bright, radiant or blazing, as transmitted from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada.

Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud note that the word wahhaj combines light and heat, while Ibn Juzayy and al-Alusi point to its strong brightness. Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan explain that the root refers to a fire kindling or a jewel shining. Al-Baghawi cites Muqatil, who says that God placed in the sun both light and heat.

Ibn 'Ashur observes that the verb "made" rather than "created" fits here, because being a blazing lamp is a state of the sun, and that the lamp image is a metaphor that brings the quality closer to the reader's mind. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that the sun's heat, felt in summer, brings many benefits to people. These points form the core of the commentators' shared reading of this verse.

This verse recounts a favour of God: He sends down abundant pouring rain, by which grain for people, pasture for livestock and dense gardens are produced. The commentators differ on the meaning of "al-mu'sirat". Ibn 'Abbas, in one transmission, Mujahid, Qatada, Muqatil and al-Kalbi understand it as the winds that press the clouds, and some support this by a reading with "bi" ("with the winds"), which Ibn 'Atiyya takes as evidence. Ibn 'Abbas in another transmission, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak, Sufyan and al-Farra' understand it as the clouds heavy with water that have not yet rained, like the young woman nearing puberty; al-Tabari prefers this view, and Ibn Kathir follows it. Al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibn Jubayr and Ubayy ibn Ka'b take it to mean the heavens, a view Ibn Kathir considers uncommon. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi note that the winds create the clouds, so the descent may be attributed to them. On "thajjaj" there is near-unanimity: water pouring out continuously and abundantly, as blood flows from sacrificed animals; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith "the best Hajj is the 'ajj and the thajj" to explain the word. The commentators read the verse as evidence of God's power and as a sign that resurrection is possible.

The plain meaning of the verse is that God sends down abundant water from the clouds, and through it brings forth grain for human food, plants for livestock, and dense gardens with interlaced trees. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that ḥabb means what is contained in the husks of harvested crops such as wheat and barley, while nabat means the pasture and herbage eaten by animals, and al-Dahhak gives the same explanation. Ikrima, reported by Ibn Abi Hatim and others, holds that the grain may be pearls in the sea and the nabat grass, a view the majority did not adopt. On the word alfaf, the commentators agree that it means gardens whose trees are intertwined and tightly packed, as al-Tabari reports from a number of early authorities. The philologists disagree about its singular: some say laff, others laffa, and al-Zamakhshari notes it may be the plural of multafifa. Al-Razi sees in the verse a proof that plant life falls into three kinds, and explains the order of mention by the relative importance of each for sustenance. Ibn 'Ashur reads it as evidence for resurrection through the revival of the earth by water. The commentators agree on the general sense and differ mainly over the nature of the grain and the linguistic origin of alfaf.

The commentators explain that this verse lists God's favours to people on earth. The abundant rain brings forth grain for food, plants for the animals, and gardens, called jannat. On the meaning of alfafan, al-Tabari and most exegetes, following Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, understand it as trees that are densely packed and intertwined. Philologists disagree about its singular: some Basran grammarians say it is laff, some Kufan ones say lafa' or lafif, and others say it has no singular, like awzaa and akhyaf. Al-Zamakhshari suggests it could be the plural of multaffa with the extra letters dropped. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi note that these gardens hold trees with varied fruits and colours. Al-Razi observes that grain is mentioned first because it is the basis of food, while gardens come last because fruit is not essential. Several commentators, including al-Biqa'i, see in these favours a proof of God's power to resurrect, since plants emerging from dead earth resemble resurrection. The commentators thus agree on the sense of the verse, which is at once a blessing and an argument.

The commentators explain that the "Day of Decision" is the Day of Resurrection, so called because God separates all creatures on it, the truthful from the false and the righteous from the wrongdoer. It is called a "mīqāt", a fixed and known appointed time with God that neither advances nor delays, a meeting-point for the first and last generations to receive reward or punishment. Most exegetes take it to mean an appointed time and tryst, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya also understand it as a limit at which the present world ends; al-Alusi finds the first reading better suited to the context. They agree on the events that precede it: the blast of the Trumpet, after which people come forth in groups, each community with its guide; the sky being opened until it becomes like gates; and the mountains being moved until they become scattered dust or like a mirage. Opinions differ on the meaning of "opened": some say the sky split to let the angels descend, while others say it breaks apart and scatters. All agree that the Trumpet is a horn, and al-Tabari cites a prophetic report to that effect.

This verse speaks of the Day of Decision, the Day of Resurrection, when the Trumpet is blown and people come forth in throngs. The commentators explain that this blast is the trumpet of resurrection by which people rise from their graves and come to the place of reckoning. They generally agree that 'afwajan' means groups and successive troops, but they differ on what these groups are. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi hold that each nation comes with its prophet or leader, citing the verse 'the day We call every people with their leader'. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Razi understand them as different groups according to their states and deeds. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Qurtubi and al-Suyuti cite the hadith of Mu'adh about categories of people gathered in various forms, but Ibn Hajar and al-Shawkani consider it weak, and al-Alusi calls it fabricated. Al-Shinqiti and Ibn 'Ashur note that the second-person form suggests these groups concern this community in particular. As for the rest of the verse, the commentators agree on the terror of that day. Al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari take the sky to open into passages, while others say it splits into pieces like planks. For the mountains, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur speak of dust scattered in the air, and Ibn Kathir of their complete disappearance, the mountains looking like a mirage.

This verse describes the sky being split open on the Day of Judgment until it becomes like many open doors. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan, take this to mean that the sky cracks and splits so that the angels can descend, as the Quran says elsewhere that the sky will be split with clouds and the angels sent down. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain that the great number of openings makes the sky appear as nothing but open doors, much like the phrase about the earth gushing forth in springs. Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi note that the verb is read in two forms, the lighter form by the Kufans and the intensified form by the others, and they discuss which suits the context better. Al-Razi observes that opening, splitting and cleaving are related but not identical ideas. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi also report that the doors may be understood as roads or paths, or as the sky broken into pieces resembling the wooden planks of doors, while the commentators do not decide between these readings. Their views agree on the image of a vast cosmic upheaval.

This verse describes the scene of the Day of Resurrection: the mountains are set in motion and removed from their places until they become like a mirage, something seen that has no real substance. The commentators explain that making the mountains move means removing them from their positions or uprooting them, and the most common understanding is that they turn into dust scattered in the air. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree that the mountains are crushed and blown away, and that the comparison with a mirage shows they vanish leaving no trace. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the point is annihilation after they have become dust, not a resemblance to water seen from a distance. Al-Razi explains that the mountains pass through several states before this: first they crumble, then they become like carded wool, then they become scattered dust, and finally they become a mirage. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Ashur stress the speed of the movement, which may be accompanied by crumbling. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi distinguish the moving of the mountains through the air at the second blast from their crumbling at the first. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Tabari note that the verse speaks of annihilation rather than of outward appearance. Most commentators rely on other verses, such as the mountains being set in motion and being ground to dust, to clarify this passage.

This verse says that Hell has been a place of ambush, a watchtower where those condemned are awaited. The commentators read it in closely related ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take it to mean that Hell lies in wait for the tyrants, those who transgressed by disbelief and injustice, and that it is their place of return and dwelling. Al-Hasan and Qatada report that it stands on the path to Paradise, so no one enters Paradise without crossing the Fire: whoever has a pass crosses, and whoever lacks one is held back. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi add that it can also be a station where angels receive the believers. Ibn Ashur links this ambush to the Day of Judgment it belongs to. The exegetes agree that the tyrants will remain in it for ahqab, long periods. Their length is disputed: Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar and Abu Hurayra give eighty years, others three hundred years or seventy thousand years, while al-Hasan stresses that no fixed number is known and that the words mean unending ages. Al-Tabari finds the sense of eternity more convincing. Most take barad to mean sleep, while Ibn Abbas understands cool drink or rest. The hamim, boiling water, and the ghassaq, the discharge from the bodies of the damned, are punishments that some would limit in time, though most take them as a lasting torment. The commentators conclude that this punishment fits the deeds of these people: disbelief, denial of the signs, and lack of fear of the reckoning.

This verse says that Hell lies in readiness as an ambush for the tyrants, those who transgress God's limits and are arrogant before their Lord, and it is their return and their dwelling. The commentators explain the word "mirsad" in closely related ways: al-Hasan and Qatada take it to mean a passage that everyone must cross before entering Paradise, Muqatil takes it to mean a place of confinement, and others understand it as a waiting place that repays each person for their deeds. The word "ma'ab" means the return or the dwelling place, as Qatada and al-Suddi say. The length of an "huqb" is greatly disputed: Ali and Abu Hurayra, reported through Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar, give eighty years, Bishr ibn Ka'b gives three hundred years, and al-Hasan gives seventy thousand years. Most of the commentators hold that the phrase means endless duration, since each period is followed by another, a view favoured by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi. Muqatil ibn Hayyan claims the verse was abrogated by "We shall increase you only in punishment", but al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi reject this, since reports cannot be abrogated. As for "bard", Mujahid, al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubayda take it to mean sleep, while al-Hasan and Ata' take it to mean rest and relief. The "ghassaq" is understood by many as the pus flowing from the bodies of the damned, by others as bitter cold, and by others as a foul stench. All agree that this punishment is a fitting recompense for their deeds, because they did not expect to be called to account and denied the signs of God.

The commentators explain the verse in its context: Hell was an ambush lying in wait for the rebellious, their place of return and dwelling, and they would remain in it for ages, tasting neither coolness nor drink except boiling water and ghassaq. Most of them, including Qatada, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir, understand 'ahqab' as successive periods without end, each age following another. As for the length of one huqb, reports differ: Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Abu Hurayra and Sa'id ibn Jubayr say eighty years, al-Hasan says seventy thousand years, Bishr ibn Ka'b three hundred years, and Qutrub a long indefinite time. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir also cite other views without settling on one. On 'barad', Mujahid, al-Suddi and Abu 'Ubayda take it to mean sleep, al-Hasan and 'Ata mean rest and relief, Ibn 'Abbas means the coolness of drink, and al-Zajjaj means cool wind, shade and sleep together. Ghassaq is taken by some as the pus of the damned or what flows from their skins, by others as zamharir, and by others as a foul stench. Some held the verse abrogated by 'We shall only increase your punishment', but al-Tabari, Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Qurtubi reply that a report cannot be abrogated; others applied it to sinful believers, a view others reject. All agree that the recompense matches the deeds, and that those who denied the reckoning and the signs of God deserve it.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the state of the rebellious in Hell, who will taste neither a coolness that eases the heat of the Fire nor a drink that quenches their thirst, except boiling water (hamim) and ghassaq. They differ on the meaning of "bard". Ibn 'Abbas, Abu 'Ubayda, al-Kisa'i, Mujahid and al-Suddi take it to mean sleep, citing a verse of al-Kindi, while al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Qatada take it to mean rest and relief. Al-Razi and others keep the literal sense of real coldness that cools the fire. Al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Ashur consider the exception discontinuous, since boiling water is not of the kind of coolness.

All agree that the hamim is extremely hot water. On the ghassaq, opinions vary: al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Nakha'i take it as the pus and discharge flowing from the bodies, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid as an intense cold that burns, and Ibn 'Umar and Ibn Zayd as an extreme stench, a hadith being cited on this. Ibn Kathir combines these, describing a foul, icy and unbearable liquid.

They also differ on the duration of the ahqab, plural of huqb. The majority take it to mean an indefinite span of time, succeeding one another without end. Others give figures: eighty years according to Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayra, Ibn Mas'ud and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, forty according to Ibn 'Amr, seventy or three hundred according to others. Al-Hasan says only God knows their number. Muqatil considers the verse abrogated, but al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir reject this, since it is a statement, not a command. The recompense matches the deeds: denial of the Resurrection and rejection of God's signs.

The commentators explain that this verse describes Hell as a mirsad, a place of ambush where its guardians lie in wait for the rebellious, and that the tawaghin are those who transgress God's limits through disbelief or wrongdoing, with Hell as their final destination. They differ on the length of the ahqab. Al-Hasan says only God knows their number, while Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hurayra hold that a huqb lasts eighty years, al-Hasan giving seventy thousand years, and al-Qurtubi reports other opinions such as forty or three hundred years. As for al-Barad, al-Tabari cites Mujahid, al-Suddi and Abu 'Ubayda, who take it to mean sleep, whereas al-Hasan and 'Ata' understand rest and relief, and Ibn 'Abbas a cool drink. All agree that the hamim is scalding water and that the ghassaq is what flows from the bodies of the damned, though they differ on its nature: al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir mention the zamharir, pus, or stench. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir note that the damned suffer both extremes of heat and cold. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir explain that the requital fits the deeds, since these people denied the resurrection and rejected God's signs. Al-Nasafi and others report Muqatil's view that the verse is abrogated, but Ibn al-Qayyim rejects it, since abrogation does not apply to a statement of fact.

The commentators explain that "jaza'an wifaqan" means the punishment the disbelievers receive in the Hereafter matches exactly their deeds and wicked words in this life, neither more nor less. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd all say the recompense corresponded to their works. Muqatil adds that the torment fits the sin, since there is no greater wrong than associating partners with God and no greater punishment than the Fire. Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir connect this phrase with the verse that follows, which gives the reason: they did not expect a reckoning because they denied the Resurrection, and they denied Our signs with great denial.

The readers differ on the form "kidhdhaban". The common reading with the doubled letter is, according to al-Farra', a Yemeni usage for the verbal noun of the intensive form. Abu 'Ubayda and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi explain the lighter reading as a mutual denial. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur develop these grammatical distinctions further.

On the substance, the commentators agree: the retribution is just and proportionate to the offence. They differ on the grammar of "wifaqan", which some treat as a verbal noun, others as an adjective meaning "fitting", and others as a reading meaning "suitable". These remarks concern the language of the verse and carry no legal consequence.

This passage explains that the punishment of the transgressors in Hell matches their deeds, and the commentators give the reason in the phrase "for they did not expect a reckoning." According to Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and most exegetes, this means they did not fear being judged by God and did not believe in the resurrection. Al-Zajjaj adds that the sense is that they did not hope for the reward of the reckoning, since they did not believe in the resurrection. Al-Razi offers several explanations, including that the word "hope" here means "expect," and that mentioning hope rather than fear points to hope prevailing in the reckoning. As for "and they denied Our signs with complete denial," the readers agree on doubling the dhal in this word, and al-Farra says this is a usage of the Yemeni dialect. The punishment is called "fitting" because, according to Muqatil, no sin is greater than polytheism and no torment greater than the Fire. The phrase "And We have recorded everything in writing" means that all deeds are registered, either in the Preserved Tablet or in the records of the angels, depending on the opinion. Finally, the words "So taste; We shall increase you only in torment" are universally regarded as the most severe verse concerning the people of the Fire, reported from Abd Allah ibn Amr, since their torment never ceases to grow.

This phrase describes the obstinacy of the disbelievers: they denied God's signs with an intense and extreme denial. It follows on from the previous clause, that they did not hope for the reckoning, so they combined rejecting the recompense with rejecting what God revealed. The commentators agree that the signs here are the verses of the Quran and what the messengers brought. On the word kidhdhaban, al-Farra' regards it as a correct Yemeni usage, a verbal noun of the form fi'al from kadhdhaba, like kharraq from kharraqa, and cites a line of verse as evidence. Al-Zajjaj and others see it as a verbal noun of mutual denial, as in men calling one another liars. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan report that the lighter reading kadhaban is attributed to 'Ali and 'Awf al-A'rabi, and al-Zamakhshari links it to kadhaba, citing a verse of al-A'sha. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan offer several grammatical analyses: an absolute object of an implied verb, of the verb itself through its implied sense, or a circumstantial accusative when read as the plural kuddhaban. Abu al-Su'ud explains that it means an excessive denial, which is why they persisted in disbelief and every kind of sin. Ibn Kathir and most commentators hold that denying the signs entails denying all of God's proofs of His oneness, of prophethood and of the return. The verse thus connects to what follows: God's recording of everything, then the words addressed to the damned, taste it, we will only increase your punishment, which 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr and Abu Hurayra report as the hardest verse concerning the people of the Fire.

The commentators explain that the verse means God has counted and recorded everything, that is, He has precisely reckoned the deeds of His servants, determined them and written them down so that nothing is lost, and this is mentioned when the punishment of the disbelievers in the Hereafter is described. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya understand the book as a precise inscription in the Preserved Tablet, while al-Razi sees in the word an emphasis on the certainty of God's knowledge, adapted to the understanding of literalists, since what is written can pass away whereas God's knowledge never does. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi treat the phrase as a circumstantial clause, meaning recorded in the Tablet or in the registers of the guardian angels. Al-Shinqiti links it to the deeds of the servants and sees in it proof of the breadth of God's knowledge down to the smallest detail, while Ibn 'Uthaymin includes both God's acts and human acts. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the expression conveys great exactness in accounting. The commentators agree that this clause is a parenthesis connecting retribution with comprehensive knowledge, and that the following verse, so taste, for We shall increase you only in punishment, is regarded by Ibn 'Abbas, Abd Allah ibn 'Amr and Abu Barza as the most severe verse concerning the people of the Fire. All agree that the punishment matches the deeds of the disbelievers, who did not hope for reckoning and denied God's signs.

The commentators explain that this verse is addressed to the people of the Fire when the punishment falls: they are told to taste the recompense for their deeds, and God will add nothing to their torment but more chastisement, a rebuke and threat matching their disbelief and denial. Al-Tabari, citing Qatada, and Ibn Kathir, citing Abdullah ibn Amr, report that this increase is endless, so they remain in ever-growing torment. Al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and others take the word “taste” to mean direct experience of the punishment, and say the chastisement is fitting to their works. They add that their fault lay in not hoping for the reckoning, meaning they did not believe in resurrection or fear the judgment, as al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada report. On denying the signs of God, al-Tabari and others understand it as rejecting God's proofs and arguments. On the word kidhdhaban, most readers take it with doubling as a verbal noun of kadhdhaba, while al-Kisai and others also accept the lighter form, and al-Zamakhshari treats it as a verbal noun of kadhaba. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that this verse was regarded as the most severe in the Qur'an for the people of the Fire, relying on the hadith of Abu Barza, though Ibn Kathir judges its chain weak. The scholars thus agree on the core meaning and differ mainly on linguistic and recitation details.

The commentators explain that the verse « Indeed, for the righteous is an achievement » means that those who fear God by obeying Him and avoiding His prohibitions will attain salvation and entry into Paradise, and will gain what they sought. Ibn Abbas understood « mafaz » as a place of recreation, while Qatada and Mujahid took it to mean deliverance from the Fire and mercy after punishment. The verse then details this achievement through gardens and grapevines: al-Tabari explains that « hada'iq » are walled orchards containing various trees, and that the mention of grapes is singled out. The « kawa'ib » are young women whose breasts are firm and rounded; Mujahid and al-Dahhak take them to be virgins, and the « atrab » are of the same age according to Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd. Regarding the cup « dihaq », opinions differ: full and overflowing according to Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada; successive according to Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid; pure according to Ikrima. There is agreement that the people of Paradise will hear neither idle talk nor lies, and al-Kisa'i read « kadhdhaban » with a lighter form, which others relate to the sense of denial. As for « ata'an hisaban », most scholars read it as a sufficient gift, while Mujahid tied it to a reward measured by deeds.

The commentators explain that the word mafaz in the verse 'Indeed, for the righteous is a place of success' means success, attaining what one seeks, and deliverance from the Fire, as Mujahid, Qatada, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state. Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak take it to mean a place of recreation. The phrase 'gardens and grapevines' is understood as an explanation of this success or as an appositive. Gardens are orchards enclosed by walls, and grapes are named separately for their excellence and abundance, with al-Tabari noting that the vines themselves are implied.

The 'kawaʿib' are, for most, young women whose breasts are firm and rounded, while al-Dahhak takes them to be virgins. The 'atrab' are of the same age, as al-Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya affirm. For the cup 'dihaq', the commentators largely agree it means full, as Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada say. Said ibn Jubayr and Mujahid take it to mean successive, and Ikrima takes it to mean pure.

On the phrase 'no idle talk nor lying', opinions differ. Ibn Abbas understands idle talk as vain speech, al-Suddi as oaths sworn while drinking, Mujahid as insults, and al-Hasan as disobedience. For lying, Said ibn Jubayr understands that they do not lie to one another, al-Hasan takes it as quarrelling, and Qatada as sin. Al-Kisa'i reads the word without doubling the letter, while al-Tabari prefers the doubled form. Ibn Kathir concludes that Paradise is free of every flaw.

Finally, the divine gift 'a sufficient reckoning' is understood by al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir as an ample and abundant gift, and by Mujahid as proportioned to deeds. The readings of 'Lord' and 'the Most Merciful' vary, and the commentators set out their reasons without deciding between them.

The commentators explain that this verse is part of the description of the bliss prepared for the God-fearing. The word kawā'ib refers to young women whose breasts are firm and rounded, and atrāb means companions of the same age. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir explain that the kawā'ib are firm-breasted young women and the atrāb are their peers in age. Al-Dahhak takes the kawā'ib to be virgins, a view reported from Qays ibn 'Asim, while Ibn Jurayj and Qatada stress the firmness of the breast. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi place the verse within the description of the Garden, and al-Razi understands the atrāb as companions of the same age. Ibn 'Ashur notes that this equality of age may refer to the women among themselves or to their relation with their husbands. All agree that these companions belong to the delights of Paradise and to its perfection. Ibn Kathir quotes a hadith from Abu Umama about the kawā'ib atrāb, and al-Alusi reports that the women of Paradise are sixteen years old according to some commentaries. Al-Tabari does not decide between these views.

The commentators explain that this verse belongs to the description of the bliss of the righteous, and that the word dihaq refers to a cup filled to the brim. This is the most widely held reading, transmitted from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd, who say the drink fills the vessel so that nothing is left empty. Al-Tabari reports that Ibn Abbas once asked his servant to pour him a dihaq and, when the cup arrived full, declared that this was exactly its meaning. Its root carries the idea of pressing and tightening, which al-Qurtubi explains, adding that the sense of succession comes close to it. Said ibn Jubayr and Mujahid, cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Mawardi, understand it as cups following one another, while Ikrima takes it to mean a clear, pure drink. Al-Razi gives first place to the sense of fullness, supporting it with Arab usage, and also mentions purity. Al-Zamakhshari takes the cup to mean the wine itself, and Ibn Ashur notes that calling the drink a cup is a familiar figure of speech. The verse continues by saying that the people of Paradise hear no idle talk or lies there, and the commentators observe that the drink of the afterlife does not intoxicate as wine does in this world. The readings of kadhdhaban, with or without doubling the letter, are discussed by al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, without any of them deciding the question definitively.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the reward of the righteous after the mention of the fate of the rebellious: in Paradise they hear neither vain speech nor lies. Most agree that their ears are kept free of empty or false words, so that they do not quarrel or accuse one another. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, followed by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, understand al-laghw as idle or false speech, while Mujahid takes it as insult, al-Hasan as sin and al-Suddi as the oath sworn while drinking wine. As for kidhdhaban, Sa'id ibn Jubayr reads it as mutual accusation of lying, al-Hasan as dispute and Qatada as sinfulness. Most readers recite the doubled form, whereas al-Kisa'i recites the single form, meaning lying or mutual denial. Al-Tabari prefers the doubled reading without rejecting the other. Ibn Kathir holds that there is no speech without benefit in Paradise, which is the abode of peace. Al-Razi takes the pronoun 'therein' to refer to the cup or to Paradise, and holds that the verse denies that its people hear any lie at all. Ibn 'Ashur sees in it a way of keeping the drink of Paradise free of the disorder that accompanies wine in this world.

The commentators explain that this verse concludes the description of the reward of the God-fearing: God gives them a recompense, and a gift from Him, which is pure bounty. Most read “ḥisāban” as “sufficient and abundant”, since one says the thing “ahsabanī” when it suffices me, while others take it as a measure proportioned to their deeds. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada report that the gift is abundant, with good deeds multiplied tenfold or seven hundredfold, and that the increase beyond the due reward is itself a favour from God. Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi keep to the sense of sufficiency and abundance, whereas al-Razi lists several meanings, including a reward owed through promise and a grace that is not owed. On the recitation, some readers gave “rabb” the genitive and “al-Rahman” the nominative, and al-Tabari prefers the genitive for “rabb” because it is closer to “rabbika”. Al-Shawkani and Ibn Kathir stress that this gift is an enduring bliss that never ends. The commentators agree that the gift is a grace from God granted according to deeds, while differing on the precise sense of “hisab”, and none of them settles the matter as the only valid reading.

This verse states that God is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and all that lies between them, the Most Merciful whose mercy encompasses everything, and that on the Day of Judgment no creature may address Him except by His permission. The commentators differ on who the pronoun in 'they possess no right to address Him' refers to. Ibn 'Abbas, through 'Ata', and al-Kalbi take it to mean the polytheists, who cannot speak to God, while believers may intercede and be heard. al-Qadi takes it to mean the believers, who have no standing to challenge God's just judgment. al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya extend it to all inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, none of whom may question God about reward or punishment. The recitations vary between nominative and genitive for 'Lord' and 'the Merciful'. Abu 'Ubayd, followed by Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari, prefers the genitive for the first word, close to 'your Lord', and the nominative for the second, which is further away, while al-Tabari considers every reading sound. All agree the scene belongs to the Day of Judgment, when speech depends on God's permission. The 'Spirit' who stands with the angels in ranks is explained in many ways: Ibn Mas'ud and, in one transmission, Ibn 'Abbas, say it is a great angel; al-Sha'bi, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak say Gabriel; Mujahid and Abu Salih describe a creature in human form who is neither angel nor human; al-Hasan and Qatada say the descendants of Adam; Zayd ibn Aslam says the Quran; al-Tabari declines to decide. Most relate 'speaks rightly' to the testimony that there is no god but God, while Mujahid and al-Dahhak take it to mean speaking the truth.

This verse describes the Day of Judgment, when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks, and no one speaks except those whom the Most Merciful permits, and who say what is right. The commentators agree on the overall sense: it is a scene of awe in which speech is bound by two conditions, divine permission and the rightness of what is said. On the identity of the Spirit, opinions differ. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, describe an angel of immense size, while al-Sha'bi and al-Dahhak identify him as Gabriel, a view al-Razi favours. Mujahid and Abu Salih describe a creation in human form that is neither angel nor man, al-Hasan and Qatada take it to mean the children of Adam, and Ibn Zayd takes it to mean the Qur'an. Al-Tabari declines to choose among these views, while Ibn Kathir leans towards the children of Adam. On what is 'right' to say, Ibn 'Abbas, Ikrima and Abu Salih understand the profession of faith, 'There is no god but God'; al-Dahhak and Mujahid understand truth; and al-Hasan understands the statement that no one enters Paradise except by mercy or Hell except by deeds. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi note that speech must be both permitted and right. The verse ends by speaking of the true day, when whoever wishes may make, through good deeds, a way back to his Lord.

The commentators explain that "that Day, the true one" refers to the Day of Resurrection, an event that is certain beyond doubt. As for "whoever wills, let him take a path of return to his Lord", they say it means that whoever wishes to be saved should take for himself a good place of return to his Lord through faith, obedience and righteous deeds. Qatada reads the word ma'ab as a path, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean a place of return. Regarding "We have warned you of a near punishment", most hold that it refers to the punishment of the Hereafter, since whatever is coming is near. Qatada and Muqatil, however, take it to be punishment in this world, such as the killing of the Quraysh at Badr. There is broad agreement that "the Day when a man sees what his hands have sent forward" means each person sees his deeds, good or bad. Al-Hasan and Qatada take "the man" to be the believer, whereas Ata' and others read it generally. The disbeliever will then wish he were dust. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari cite reports from Abu Hurayra and Ibn Amr about the judgment among animals, after which they are turned to dust, so the disbeliever wishes to be like them. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi also mention the view that the disbeliever here is Iblis, who scorned being created from clay. Al-Razi notes that the verse does not deny that deeds are the cause of reward and punishment, which operates by divine promise and decree. All agree that the passage urges doing good before it is too late.

This verse warns of a near punishment, the punishment of the Hereafter, since whatever is coming is near. On that day every person sees what their hands have done, good or evil, and the disbeliever wishes he were dust. The commentators agree on the warning and on the great anguish it describes. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take 'the person' to mean people in general, while al-Hasan and Qatada take it to mean the believer, who sees his deeds without knowing his final fate. According to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, the disbeliever sees his works and wishes he had never been created or raised. The wish to be dust is explained, in several reports from Abu Hurayra and Ibn Umar, by the judgment among animals, after which they are turned to dust, and the disbeliever envies them. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention this explanation. Some, such as al-Baghawi, al-Razi, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan, report that the disbeliever may be Iblis, who scorned Adam for being made of clay and would then wish to be made of the same substance. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi consider it more sound to read the term as covering every disbeliever. The commentators thus differ on who 'the person' and 'the disbeliever' are, and on the exact meaning of dust, but they agree on the seriousness of the warning.
